repos.readme:
kafka-lag-lab

A Kafka consumer-lag bottleneck lab: reproduce real causes of growing
consumer lag on purpose, watch them happen, then fix them — all against a
real, running Kafka cluster.

The question this project answers: a consumer group's lag is climbing
fast, consumers are already scaled horizontally, and the instinct is
"just add more consumers." But that only helps if consumer-vs-partition
count is actually the constraint. This project makes the other possible
causes — key skew, slow processing, retry storms, rebalance thrashing —
concrete and reproducible, so the difference is something you can see
rather than just reason about.

Architecture

kafka-lag-lab/
├── docker-compose.yml     # Kafka (KRaft mode) + topic-init
├── pom.xml                # Maven multi-module parent
├── producer/              # configurable-rate, configurable-key-strategy producer
├── consumer/              # configurable-processing-mode consumer
├── diagnose/              # auto-diagnosis of which bottleneck is active
└── scripts/
    ├── run-scenario.ps1   # drives producer/consumer/diagnose per named scenario
    ├── watch-lag.sh       # live per-partition lag table
    └── watch-lag-skew.sh  # live lag-skew ratio (max/avg)
  • Kafka: single-broker KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper), confluentinc/cp-kafka:8.0.0
  • Topic: lag-lab-events, explicitly created with 6 partitions
    (auto-create is disabled — partition count is a deliberate variable)
  • Producer / Consumer / Diagnose: plain Java 21 + kafka-clients, no
    Spring — kept lean since the point is the Kafka mechanics
  • Producer and consumer each use a small strategy pattern: which key
    strategy or message-processing behavior runs is selected by an
    environment variable at startup, so each scenario lives in its own class
    (producer/strategy/, consumer/processing/)

Requirements

  • Docker + Docker Compose
  • Java 21, Maven

Quick start

# 1. Start Kafka and create the topic
docker compose up -d

# 2. Build everything
mvn clean install

# 3. Run the baseline consumer
java -jar consumer/target/consumer-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

# 4. In another terminal, run the baseline producer
java -jar producer/target/producer-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

# 5. In a third terminal, watch lag live
./scripts/watch-lag.sh

With no environment variables set, this is the baseline: even key
distribution, fast processing, lag should stay flat and near-zero across
all 6 partitions.

Running scenarios

scripts/run-scenario.ps1 sets the right environment variables for a
named scenario and launches the given role. Run the same scenario name
as -Role consumer and -Role producer in separate terminals; add
-Role diagnose in a third for a live verdict.

# one-time per PowerShell session
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass

# Terminal 1
.\scripts\run-scenario.ps1 -Role consumer -Scenario retry-storm

# Terminal 2
.\scripts\run-scenario.ps1 -Role producer -Scenario retry-storm

# Terminal 3 (optional)
.\scripts\run-scenario.ps1 -Role diagnose -Scenario retry-storm
Scenario Root cause What you should see
baseline — Flat, low lag on all 6 partitions
hot-partition One key gets disproportionate traffic, pinning it to one partition One partition climbs steadily, others stay flat
hot-partition-fixed Same entity, key salted across buckets All 6 partitions flat again
slow-processing Consumer blocks synchronously per message All 6 partitions climb evenly
slow-processing-fixed Same work, fanned out across a thread pool Lag stabilizes and drains
retry-storm Unbounded retries, no backoff cap Lag climbs, one bad message can stall a batch
retry-storm-fixed Capped attempts + exponential backoff + simulated DLQ Lag stays bounded; occasional DLQ: giving up... lines
rebalance-thrashing Batch processing time exceeds max.poll.interval.ms Repeated [REBALANCE] log lines
rebalance-thrashing-fixed Smaller batches or concurrent processing [REBALANCE] lines stop appearing

For the last three pairs, the producer config never changes — only the
consumer needs restarting between problem and fix. Only hot-partition*
requires restarting the producer too.

Auto-diagnosis

The diagnose module samples lag over a short rolling window and
classifies the active bottleneck using the same signals in the table
above: rebalance events (checked first, since thrashing can masquerade as
a processing slowdown), skew ratio between the worst and average
partition, and how erratic lag growth is step-to-step.

java -jar consumer/target/consumer-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar | Tee-Object -FilePath consumer.log
java -jar diagnose/target/diagnose-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

Tunable via env vars: GROUP_ID, KAFKA_CONTAINER, BOOTSTRAP_SERVER,
INTERVAL_SECONDS (default 3), SAMPLES (default 5), REBALANCE_LOG.

Known limitations

  • The diagnosis thresholds (skew ratio, step-delta erraticness) are
    hand-tuned against this project's own traffic rates — a demonstration
    of the approach, not a production-grade classifier. In particular, at
    default parameters a mild retry storm can average out to look
    statistically similar to a smooth slow-processing bottleneck once
    batched — worth trying a higher RETRY_FAILURE_RATE to see the
    distinction sharpen.
  • Everything runs against a single-broker cluster; multi-broker
    replication and rebalancing add failure modes this project doesn't cover.
  • Lag observability is deliberately simple (polling
    kafka-consumer-groups --describe); a production setup would use
    Prometheus/Grafana or Kafka's own JMX metrics instead.

What this project demonstrates

"Add more consumers" is only correct if consumer-vs-partition count is
actually the constraint. Key skew, slow downstream calls, unbounded
retries, and rebalance churn all produce the same visible symptom — rising
lag — from different causes, and each needs a different fix. The goal
here was to make that difference something you can reproduce and observe,
not just reason about.

A comprehensive Task Manager API built with Spring Boot, demonstrating three different persistence strategies - from simple in-memory storage
to production-ready Docker deployment.

🎯 Project Overview

This project showcases three progressive versions of the same Task Manager API, each adding more complexity and production-ready features:

  • Version 1: Simple in-memory storage - Perfect for understanding REST API basics
  • Version 2: H2 database with JPA - Database integration with automatic schema generation
  • Version 3: MySQL with Docker - Three deployment scenarios (local, mixed, fully containerized)

📋 Table of Contents

  • 🚀 Quick Start
  • 📁 Project Structure
  • 📊 Versions Comparison
  • 🚀 Version 1: In-Memory
  • 💾 Version 2: H2 Database
  • 🐳 Version 3: MySQL with Docker
  • 🔧 API Endpoints (All Versions)
  • 🧪 Testing
  • 💻 System Requirements
  • 🔧 Troubleshooting

🚀 Quick Start

Clone and Build All Versions

git clone <your-repo-url>
cd java-multimodule-springboot-taskmanager-lab

# Build all modules
mvn clean install

Run Individual Versions

Version Command Port Access URL
v1 (In-Memory) cd version1-inmemory && mvn spring-boot:run 8080 http://localhost:8080/api/tasks
v2 (H2) cd version2-h2 && mvn spring-boot:run 8081 http://localhost:8081/api/tasks
v3 (MySQL/Docker) See Version 3 section 8082 http://localhost:8082/api/tasks

│
├── pom.xml                          # Parent POM configuration
│
├── version1-inmemory/               # 🚀 Simplest version

│   └── pom.xml                      # Spring Web only
│

Feature Version 1 Version 2 Version 3
Port 8080 8081 8082

Spring AOP Basics Tutorial

A comprehensive, hands-on guide to learning Spring AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) through practical examples. This multi-module project covers all essential AOP concepts from XML-based configuration to advanced programmatic usage.

SUMMARY OF THE PROJECT

📋 Table of Contents

# Module Description Key Concepts
1 Spring-AOP-XML Traditional XML-based AOP configuration XML schema-based aspects, pointcut definitions, declarative configuration
2 Spring-AOP-AspectJ AspectJ annotation-based AOP @aspect, @before, @after, @around, pointcut expressions
3 Spring-AOP-Around-and-AOP Deep dive into @around advice ProceedingJoinPoint, method interception, execution control
4 Spring-AOP-normal-execution AOP in standard execution flow Join points, method invocation, proxy mechanics
5 Spring-AOP-exceptions Exception handling with AOP @AfterThrowing, exception translation, error logging
6 Spring-AOP-CrossCutting-Caching-and-Exception Practical cross-cutting concerns Caching implementation, exception handling patterns
7 Spring-AOP-CrossCutting-normal-execution Cross-cutting concerns in normal flow Logging, security, transaction management
8 Spring-AOP-programmatically-and-declaratively Programmatic vs Declarative AOP ProxyFactory, AspectJProxyFactory, dynamic proxy creation
9 Spring-AOP-RealWorld-Integration-Case Spring AOP A practical, end-to-end case study demonstrating multiple aspects working together

🎯 What is Spring AOP?

Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) complements Object-Oriented Programming by providing a way to modularize cross-cutting concerns—functionality that affects multiple parts of an application (logging, security, transactions).

Key Benefits:

  • Separation of Concerns: Keep business logic clean from technical concerns
  • DRY Principle: Write cross-cutting logic once, apply everywhere
  • Maintainability: Centralize common functionality
  • Flexibility: Enable/disable aspects without changing business code

Core Concepts:

Concept Definition Example
Aspect A module that encapsulates cross-cutting concerns @Aspect class LoggingAspect
Join Point A point in program execution where an aspect can be applied Method execution, object instantiation
Advice Action taken by an aspect at a join point @before, @after, @around
Pointcut Predicate that matches join points execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))
Weaving Process of applying aspects to target objects Compile-time, load-time, or runtime
Target Object Object being advised by aspects Your service or repository classes
AOP Proxy Object created by AOP framework JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB proxy

Advice Types:

Method Execution Timeline:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ @Around (before part)                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ @Before                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ >>> Actual Method Execution <<<         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ @AfterReturning OR @AfterThrowing       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ @After (finally)                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ @Around (after part)                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

🏗️ Project Structure

This is a Maven multi-module project using Spring Framework 6.1.15 (LTS) and Java 17.

Prerequisites:

  • Java 17 or higher
  • Maven 3.6+
  • IDE (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code)

Building the Project:

mvn clean install

Running Individual Modules:

cd <module-name>
mvn clean test

📦 Module Details & Common Patterns Across All Modules

Package Structure

src/main/java/com/vbforge/
├── model/          # Domain models
├── service/        # Business logic (clean!)
├── aspect/         # Cross-cutting concerns
├── annotation/     # Custom annotations (if needed)
├── exception/      # Custom exceptions
├── context/        # Context holders (like SecurityContext)
└── MainApp.java    # Demo application

POM Dependencies (All Modules)

<dependencies>
    <!-- Core -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-aspects</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.aspectj</groupId>
        <artifactId>aspectjweaver</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Jakarta Annotations -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>jakarta.annotation</groupId>
        <artifactId>jakarta.annotation-api</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Logging -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
        <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
        <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Testing -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
        <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

🎯 Key Learning Purposes

1. Spring-AOP-XML

Purpose: Learn traditional XML-based AOP configuration (Spring 2.0 style)

What you'll learn: <aop:config>, <aop:aspect>, <aop:pointcut>, XML-based advice declarations

2. Spring-AOP-AspectJ

Purpose: Modern annotation-based AOP with @AspectJ syntax

What you'll learn: @Aspect, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Pointcut

3. Spring-AOP-Around-and-AOP

Purpose: Master the most powerful advice type - @around

What you'll learn: ProceedingJoinPoint, proceed(), execution control, return value modification

4. Spring-AOP-normal-execution

Purpose: Understand AOP in standard application execution flow

What you'll learn: Join point mechanics, proxy behavior, method invocation chains

5. Spring-AOP-exceptions

Purpose: Exception handling and recovery with AOP

What you'll learn: @AfterThrowing, exception translation, retry logic, error logging

6. Spring-AOP-CrossCutting-Caching-and-Exception

Purpose: Real-world cross-cutting concerns - caching and exception handling

What you'll learn: Custom caching aspect, exception handling patterns, cache eviction

7. Spring-AOP-CrossCutting-normal-execution

Purpose: Logging, security, and transaction management in normal execution

What you'll learn: Performance monitoring, audit logging, security aspects

8. Spring-AOP-programmatically-and-declaratively

Purpose: Compare programmatic and declarative AOP approaches

What you'll learn: ProxyFactory, AspectJProxyFactory, dynamic proxy creation, advisor chains

9. Spring-AOP-RealWorld-Integration-Case

Purpose: Everything come together in a production-like scenario

What you'll learn: Logging, Performance, Security, Transactions, Exception Handling, Auditing

📚 Common Pointcut Expressions Reference

// All methods in a package
execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))

// Methods starting with "get"
execution(* get*(..))

// Methods in classes ending with "Service"
execution(* *Service.*(..))

// Public methods only
execution(public * *(..))

// Methods with specific return type
execution(String *(..))

// Methods with specific parameters
execution(* *(*String, int))

// Methods with annotation
@annotation(com.example.MyAnnotation)

// All methods in annotated classes
@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)

// Combine with AND
execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..)) && @annotation(Transactional)

// Combine with OR
execution(* save*(..)) || execution(* update*(..))

// Exclude certain methods
execution(* *(..)) && !execution(* toString())

repos.readme:
workshop-kafka-apps

Hands-on Kafka workshop built with Spring Boot 3, Thymeleaf, and Docker (KRaft mode — no ZooKeeper).
Each project is a standalone application targeting a real-world Kafka pattern, progressing from zero to production-ready knowledge.

Goal

Most Kafka tutorials stop at "send and receive a string." This workshop doesn't.

The focus is on patterns that actually appear in production Java systems — reliable messaging, error handling, offset commit strategies, exactly-once semantics, and event sourcing. By the end, you will have practical, interview-ready knowledge of the producer/consumer API without getting lost in cluster internals or Kafka Streams DSL.

Projects

# Project Key Kafka Concepts
1 kafka-01-java-code-beginners Producers and Consumers using Java, showcasing various patterns including simple messaging, callbacks, key-based partitioning, graceful shutdown, and cooperative rebalancing. Configured with Kafka in Docker (+ Conduktor UI) (pure Java)
2 kafka-02-learning-scenarios 5 progressive scenarios: basic messaging → load balancing → keyed messages → manual offsets → complete e-commerce pipeline using pure Java Kafka client (pure Java)
3 kafka-03-echo-bot KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener, auto-commit, topic creation (Spring Boot)
4 kafka-04-dashboard Consumer groups, partition awareness, in-memory aggregation, WebSocket streaming (Spring Boot)
5 kafka-05-notification-demo A simple Spring Boot demo application demonstrating Apache Kafka (Kafka and Zookeeper using Docker) integration with Thymeleaf for sending and consuming notifications. (Spring Boot)
6 kafka-06-producer-consumer-masterclass Comprehensive Spring Boot + Kafka masterclass covering every producer/consumer pattern used in real projects: sync, async, keyed, filtered, transactional, error-handling, and manual offset control. (Spring Boot)
7 kafka-07-producer-consumer-separate-modules Multi-module Spring Boot Kafka solution featuring separate producer-consumer architecture, KRaft broker, idempotent processing with caching, and Docker Compose orchestration. (Spring Boot)
8 kafka-08-simple-producer-consumer Basic producer-consumer, JSON serialization, topic auto-creation

Potential projects (planning):

  • kafka-order-logger (Idempotent producer, exactly-once semantics, ErrorHandlingDeserializer, offset commit to DB)
  • kafka-shopping-cart (Compacted topics, event sourcing, state reconstruction, snapshotting)
  • kafka-dlq-visualizer (@RetryableTopic, poison pills, manual DLQ replay, dead letter queue patterns)
  • kafka-event-sourcing-pattern (Event sourcing pattern)
  • kafka-exactly-once-streams (Exactly-once with Kafka Streams)

Tech Stack

Tool Version Purpose
Java 17 / 21 Application runtime
Spring Boot 3.4.x Application framework
Spring Kafka (managed by Boot) Kafka producer/consumer abstraction
Apache Kafka KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper) Message broker
Thymeleaf + WebSocket (managed by Boot) Server-side UI with live updates
Docker + Docker Compose Latest Local Kafka + Conduktor setup
Maven 3.9+ Build tool

Learning Scope

This workshop is intentionally scoped. Here is exactly what will and won't be covered — and why.

Priority Topic
✅ Must Produce and consume messages with Spring Boot
✅ Must Topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups
✅ Must application.yml configuration for producers and consumers
✅ Must Commit strategies: auto-commit vs manual ack
✅ Must Error handling: retries, ErrorHandlingDeserializer, poison pills
✅ Must Dead letter queues and @RetryableTopic
✅ Should Idempotent producer and exactly-once semantics
✅ Should Consumer rebalancing and partition assignment
✅ Should Event sourcing pattern with Kafka as the event log
❌ Skip for now Kafka Streams DSL and state stores
❌ Skip for now Cluster administration and KRaft internals
❌ Skip for now Schema Registry and Avro serialization

Rule of thumb: master the producer/consumer API with proper error handling — that is what 90% of real projects use day to day.

Running the Projects

Option A — Shared Kafka instance

If you already have Kafka running on localhost:9092, skip the per-project Docker Compose and point each app at it via application.yml. This is the normal development workflow once your environment is stable.

Option B — Per-project Docker Compose (mostly used across repository projects)

Each project ships its own docker-compose.yml with Kafka in KRaft mode and a Conduktor UI panel.

cd kafka-echo-bot
docker compose up -d
./mvnw spring-boot:run

Conduktor UI is available at http://localhost:8085 for visual inspection of topics, consumer groups, and offsets.

  • Maven 3.9+ (or use the ./mvnw wrapper)
  • Basic Spring Boot knowledge: controllers, services, application.yml
  • No prior Kafka experience required — that is what this workshop is for

repos.description: Simple flow with Docker & Jenkins (CICD)
repos.readme:
simple-health-check-cicd

A minimal Spring Boot service built as a hands-on exercise in shipping a real CI/CD pipeline end to end: code → GitHub → Jenkins (build, test, image, push) → Docker Hub → pullable by anyone.

The app itself is intentionally small — the point of this project is the pipeline, not the business logic.

  • GitHub: vbforge/simple-health-check-cicd
  • Docker Hub: vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd

Endpoints

Method Path Returns
GET /ping pong — plain smoke-test endpoint
GET /info {"name": "...", "version": "..."} — app name/version as JSON
GET /actuator/health {"status": "UP"} — Spring Actuator health check

Running this project

Pull the published image directly (no build needed):

docker pull vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd:latest
docker run -p 8080:8080 vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd:latest

Or a specific version:

docker pull vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd:0.1.0
docker run -p 8080:8080 vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd:0.1.0

Then:

curl localhost:8080/ping
curl localhost:8080/info
curl localhost:8080/actuator/health

Or run from source locally:

./mvnw spring-boot:run

Or build the image yourself:

docker build -t simple-health-check-cicd:local .
docker run -p 8080:8080 simple-health-check-cicd:local

No database, no external dependencies — this service is fully self-contained.

Tech stack

  • Java 21
  • Spring Boot 3.3 (Web, Actuator)
  • Maven (with wrapper — no local Maven install required)
  • Multi-stage Docker build (eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine → eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine)
  • Jenkins (declarative pipeline, multibranch job)

CI/CD Pipeline

Build, test, image, and publish are fully automated via Jenkins — see Jenkinsfile.

Pipeline stages:

Checkout -> Build & Unit Test -> Docker Build -> Docker Push (main only)
  • Every branch (feature branches, PRs) is built and unit-tested by Jenkins automatically.
  • Only main triggers Docker Build + Docker Push — feature branches never publish an image.
  • The published image is tagged with the version from pom.xml (e.g. 0.1.0), plus latest. Not a raw build number — the Docker tag, the git tag, and the pom version all agree.

Release flow used for every new feature:

1. git checkout -b feature/<name>
2. develop + write tests
3. push branch -> Jenkins builds + tests (no image push)
4. bump version in pom.xml
5. open PR -> merge to main
6. Jenkins builds, tests, builds image, pushes vladbogdadocker/simple-health-check-cicd:<version> + :latest
7. git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z

Versioning follows Semantic Versioning: new capability → MINOR bump, fix → PATCH, breaking change → MAJOR. Commits follow Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:, etc.) so git history itself doubles as a changelog.

Jenkins Setup (from scratch)

This section documents exactly how the Jenkins instance behind this pipeline was configured, so it's reproducible rather than tribal knowledge.

1. Running Jenkins with Docker access

Jenkins runs as its own container, separate from this project, via a standalone infra docker-compose.yml:

version: "3.8"

services:
  jenkins:
    container_name: jenkins
    image: jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21
    user: root   # simplest way to get read/write access to the mounted docker.sock locally
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
      - "50000:50000"
    volumes:
      - jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock   # lets Jenkins talk to the host's Docker daemon

volumes:
  jenkins_home:

Mounting the host's Docker socket (Docker-outside-of-Docker) lets the Jenkins container run docker build / docker push against the host daemon directly, without nested Docker-in-Docker overhead. Running as root avoids socket-permission friction on a local, single-user setup.

The base jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21 image doesn't ship the Docker CLI — it was verified/installed inside the container so pipeline sh steps could actually call docker.

2. Credentials (Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials)

Two credentials were added:

ID Kind Used for
dockerhub-creds Username with password Docker Hub push. Password = a Docker Hub access token (Account Settings → Security), never the account password.
github-creds Username with password Authenticating GitHub API calls. Password = a GitHub Personal Access Token (Contents: Read-only, Metadata: Read-only for a public repo).

github-creds was added after hitting GitHub's anonymous API rate limit (60 requests/hour) during branch scanning, which made Jenkins throttle itself heavily. Authenticated requests get 5,000/hour — attaching this credential to the job's branch source fixed it.

3. The multibranch pipeline job

Jenkins → New Item → name: simple-health-check-cicd → type: Multibranch Pipeline.

  • Branch Sources → GitHub
    • Repository URL: https://github.com/vbforge/simple-health-check-cicd.git
    • Credentials: github-creds
  • Build Configuration: by Jenkinsfile, script path Jenkinsfile (default — matches root location)
  • Scan Repository Triggers: periodic scan (manual "Scan Repository Now" used during setup/testing; can be shortened to poll every few minutes, or replaced with a GitHub webhook if Jenkins is ever hosted somewhere reachable from the internet)

Multibranch (rather than a plain Pipeline job) was chosen so every feature/* branch and PR gets discovered and built automatically, without creating a new job per branch.

4. Gotchas hit and fixed along the way

  • ./mvnw: Permission denied — the Maven wrapper lost its executable bit in git. Fixed by forcing the mode directly into git's index (works even when core.fileMode is false locally): 
    git update-index --chmod=+x mvnw
git commit -m "fix: make mvnw executable"
git push
  • New branches not appearing in Jenkins — periodic scanning isn't instant; a manual "Scan Repository Now" (or a shorter poll interval) is needed to pick up a freshly pushed branch without a webhook.
  • Branch scan stuck "sleeping" — caused by the anonymous GitHub API rate limit described above; resolved by attaching github-creds to the branch source.

repos.name: books-tracker
repos.description: A role-based web application for managing home book collection. Deployed on AWS.
repos.readme:
📚 Books Tracker

A personal library management system for tracking your technical book collection.
Upload, organize, and read PDF and EPUB books directly in the browser, with per-user
reading progress, bookmarks, tags, and domain-based organization.

Screenshots:

Features

  • In-browser reader — PDF (PDF.js) and EPUB (epub.js) with page/progress tracking
  • Reading progress — auto-saved on every page turn, restored on next open
  • Bookmarks — up to 50 bookmarks per book (PDF), instant navigation
  • Book organization — domains (e.g. Java, DevOps), difficulty levels, personal tags
  • Cover images — upload or auto-display without a cover
  • User system — registration, login, role-based access (USER / ADMIN)
  • Admin panel — upload books, manage domains and tags, view statistics, export library
  • Responsive — desktop, tablet, landscape mobile supported
  • Dark / light theme — persisted per browser
  • 3 storage backends — local disk, MinIO (Docker), AWS S3
  • One-command Docker stacks — MySQL + storage + app, no manual startup needed

Tech Stack

Layer Technology
Language Java 17
Framework Spring Boot 3.5
Templates Thymeleaf + Thymeleaf Security Extras
Security Spring Security (session-based, CSRF enabled)
ORM Spring Data JPA + Hibernate
Database MySQL 8 (H2 for tests)
File storage Local disk / MinIO / AWS S3
PDF reader PDF.js 3.11 (CDN)
EPUB reader epub.js + JSZip (CDN)
MIME detection Apache Tika
Build tool Maven
Utilities Lombok, Apache Commons IO
Containerization Docker, Docker Compose (multi-service stacks)

Project Structure

books-tracker/
├── Dockerfile                     # Multi-stage build for the app container
├── docker-compose.yml             # MinIO only (run the app natively)
├── docker-compose.full.yml        # MySQL + MinIO + App — one command, full stack
├── docker-compose.local.yml       # MySQL + App + local disk storage — one command
├── start-local.bat / .sh          # Double-click/run to bring docker-compose.local.yml up
├── stop-local.bat / .sh           # Double-click/run to stop it (data preserved)
├── home-library/                  # Created on first run — books land here (local Docker profile)
│
src/main/java/com/vbforge/bookstracker/
├── config/          # Spring configuration (Security, Storage, MinIO, S3, WebMvc)
├── controller/      # MVC controllers + REST API for the reader
├── dto/             # Data Transfer Objects
├── entity/          # JPA entities (Book, User, Tag, Domain, ReadingProgress)
├── exception/       # Custom exceptions + WebExceptionHandler
├── repository/      # Spring Data JPA repositories
└── service/
    ├── StorageService.java       # Storage abstraction interface
    └── impl/
        ├── LocalStorageService   # Disk storage
        ├── MinioStorageService   # MinIO (S3-compatible)
        └── S3StorageService      # AWS S3

src/main/resources/
├── application.yml               # Shared config + active profile switch
├── application-local.yml         # Local disk profile
├── application-minio.yml         # MinIO profile
├── application-s3.yml            # AWS S3 profile
├── static/                       # CSS, JS, images
└── templates/                    # Thymeleaf HTML templates

Prerequisites

  • Java 17+
  • Maven 3.8+
  • MySQL 8 running locally (not needed if using the full Docker stacks below)
  • Docker Desktop — needed for the minio profile, and for either full Docker stack

Quick Start

1. Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/your-username/books-tracker.git
cd books-tracker

2. Set up the database

MySQL must be running. The app creates the database automatically on first startup
via createDatabaseIfNotExist=true in the JDBC URL. No manual SQL needed.

Default credentials in the config files: root / 11111111 — change these to match
your local MySQL setup in the relevant application-{profile}.yml.

3. Choose a storage profile

There are three profiles. Set spring.profiles.active in application.yml:

spring:
  profiles:
    active: local   # or: minio, s3

Prefer not to juggle profiles and manual startup at all? Skip straight to
Running Everything in Docker below —
one command starts MySQL, storage, and the app together.

Storage Profiles

local — Files on disk (simplest, no Docker)

Edit application-local.yml:

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/books_tracker?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true&...
    username: root
    password: your_password

library:
  storage-path: C:/your/path/to/home-library   # Windows
  # storage-path: /home/user/home-library       # Linux / Mac

Files are stored under storage-path/<domain-folder>/<filename>.
Covers are stored under storage-path/covers/.

Set profiles.active: local and run — no other setup needed.

minio — MinIO Docker (S3-compatible, local object storage)

MinIO behaves exactly like AWS S3 but runs locally. Good for development.

1. Start MinIO:

docker-compose up -d

This starts MinIO on:

  • http://localhost:9000 — S3 API (Spring Boot connects here)
  • http://localhost:9001 — Web console (browse files, check buckets)
  • Login: minioadmin / minioadmin

The books bucket is auto-created on first app startup. No manual setup.

2. Configure application-minio.yml:

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/books_tracker_minio?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true&...
    username: root
    password: your_password

app:
  storage:
    minio:
      url:        http://localhost:9000
      access-key: minioadmin
      secret-key: minioadmin
      bucket:     books

Set profiles.active: minio and run.

Note on where MinIO data physically lives: it's stored in a Docker-managed named
volume, not a folder you chose. On Windows/Docker Desktop (WSL2 backend) that
volume sits inside the WSL2 virtual disk, not a plain Windows folder — use the
MinIO console at localhost:9001, or docker volume inspect, to get at it. This
is one of the reasons docker-compose.local.yml (below) exists — it gives you
the same "files really are right there" access as the local profile, but with
MySQL and the app also containerized.

s3 — AWS S3 (production)

1. Create an S3 bucket in AWS Console:

  • S3 → Create bucket
  • Name: must be globally unique (e.g. books-tracker-yourname)
  • Region: pick one close to you
  • Block all public access: ON (default — keep it)

2. Create IAM credentials:

  • IAM → Security credentials → Access keys → Create
  • Use case: "Local code"
  • Copy both the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key

3. Configure application-s3.yml:

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/books_tracker_s3?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true&...
    username: root
    password: your_password

app:
  storage:
    s3:
      region:     eu-central-1          # match your bucket's region
      bucket:     books-tracker-yourname
      access-key: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
      secret-key: wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY

Set profiles.active: s3 and run. The app validates the bucket exists on startup
and fails fast with a clear error if the credentials or bucket name are wrong.

Note: Each profile uses its own isolated database (books_tracker,
books_tracker_minio, books_tracker_s3). Data is never mixed between profiles.

Running Everything in Docker (One Command)

Two additional compose files remove the need to run MySQL and the app manually.
Both build the app from the included Dockerfile (multi-stage: Maven build → JRE
runtime) and wire it up to the other containers automatically. Neither requires a
new Spring profile — they reuse the existing minio/local profiles and override
just the hostnames/paths via environment variables, the same override mechanism
already used in Environment Variables (Production)
below. This keeps the profile-to-storage-backend mapping simple: local/minio/s3
still mean exactly what they always meant.

Compose file Starts Storage profile Where books land
docker-compose.yml MinIO only (app runs natively) minio Docker-managed volume
docker-compose.full.yml MySQL + MinIO + App minio Docker-managed volume
docker-compose.local.yml MySQL + App local ./home-library on your host disk

docker-compose.full.yml — MySQL + MinIO + App

docker-compose -f docker-compose.full.yml up -d --build
  • App: http://localhost:8080
  • MinIO console: http://localhost:9001 (minioadmin / minioadmin)
  • MySQL: localhost:3307 (root / 11111111) — remapped to 3307 since a native
    MySQL install commonly already owns 3306 on the host; internally, containers
    still reach it at mysql:3306
  • Rebuild after code changes: docker-compose -f docker-compose.full.yml up -d --build app
  • Stop (data kept): docker-compose -f docker-compose.full.yml down
  • Full reset (wipes DB + MinIO data): docker-compose -f docker-compose.full.yml down -v

docker-compose.local.yml — MySQL + App, local disk storage

Same idea, but storage stays on disk instead of MinIO, matching the local
profile. library.storage-path is overridden to a container path
(/app/home-library) that's bind-mounted to ./home-library on the host, so
uploaded files are visible directly in Windows Explorer / Finder — no volume
inspection needed.

Start / stop scripts (double-click from Explorer, or run from Git Bash/WSL):

Script What it does
start-local.bat / start-local.sh Builds and starts the stack
stop-local.bat / stop-local.sh Stops containers — database and books are preserved for next start

Or run directly:

docker-compose -f docker-compose.local.yml up -d --build   # start
docker-compose -f docker-compose.local.yml down             # stop (data kept)
docker-compose -f docker-compose.local.yml down -v          # full reset, wipes DB (home-library folder is untouched — it's a bind mount, not a volume)
  • App: http://localhost:8080
  • MySQL: localhost:3307 (root / 11111111)
  • Books: ./home-library (real folder, next to the compose file)

Only run one Docker stack at a time. docker-compose.full.yml and
docker-compose.local.yml reuse the same container names
(bookstracker-mysql, bookstracker-app). If you're switching from one to
the other, stop the first one before starting the second.

Running the Application

mvn spring-boot:run

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser.

On first startup, DataSeeder creates:

  • An admin account (password: admin) with the ADMIN role
  • An user account (password: user) with the USER role
  • A set of default domains (Java Core, Spring, DevOps, etc.)

Change the default passwords immediately after first login.

Build a runnable JAR

mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/bookstracker-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

To run with a specific profile via command line:

java -jar target/bookstracker-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=s3

Running Tests

Tests use an H2 in-memory database — no MySQL, no MinIO, no Docker needed.

mvn test

The test suite includes:

  • Unit tests — BookServiceTest, ReadingProgressServiceTest (Mockito, no Spring context)
  • Integration tests — BookControllerTest, ReadingApiControllerTest (MockMvc + H2)

Coverage: file validation, upload/delete cascades, tag ownership, progress tracking,
bookmark limits, access control, and user isolation.

Supported File Formats

Format In-browser reading Download
PDF ✅ PDF.js reader ✅
EPUB ✅ epub.js reader ✅
MOBI ❌ (download only) ✅
DJVU ❌ (download only) ✅

Maximum upload size: 80 MB per file.

Key Endpoints

Method URL Description
GET / Dashboard
GET /books Book list (search, filter, paginate)
GET /books/{id} Book detail
GET /books/{id}/read In-browser reader
GET /books/{id}/download Download file
GET /books/{id}/stream Stream file inline (used by epub.js)
GET /api/reading/{id}/progress Get reading progress (JSON)
POST /api/reading/{id}/progress Save reading progress (JSON)
POST /api/reading/{id}/bookmarks/add Add bookmark
POST /api/reading/{id}/bookmarks/remove Remove bookmark
GET /admin/books/upload Upload form (ADMIN only)
GET /admin/stats Statistics (ADMIN only)
GET /admin/books/export/csv Export library as CSV (ADMIN only)

Security

  • Session-based authentication (30-minute timeout)
  • CSRF protection enabled on all state-changing requests
  • Role-based access: ADMIN can upload, edit, delete books and manage domains/tags
  • USER can read books, track progress, manage personal tags
  • All file downloads require authentication — files are never served as public static resources
  • Passwords stored with BCrypt

Architecture Notes

Storage abstraction

StorageService is an interface with three implementations selected by Spring profile.
Controllers and services depend only on the interface — switching from local disk
to S3 requires only a config change, no code changes.

Reading progress

Progress is stored per user per book in ReadingProgress. For PDFs, currentPage
and totalPages are stored as integers. For EPUBs, currentPage stores a percentage
(0–100) and totalPages is always 100. The "Continue Reading" widget on the dashboard
uses progressPercent which works correctly for both formats.

Profile isolation

Each storage profile uses a separate MySQL database. This prevents data mixing
during development — you can switch freely between profiles without stale data
from another backend appearing in your UI.

Containerized app, native profiles

The Docker full-stack files (docker-compose.full.yml, docker-compose.local.yml)
deliberately don't introduce new Spring profiles. They run the app with the same
minio/local profile it would use natively, and override only the
hostnames/paths that differ inside a container (mysql/minio service names
instead of localhost, a bind-mounted storage path instead of a native Windows
path). This keeps application-{profile}.yml as the single source of truth for
what each storage backend looks like, with the compose files responsible only for
where things run — not what they mean.

Environment Variables (Production)

For production deployments, use environment variables instead of hardcoding
credentials in yml files:

SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:mysql://your-rds-host:3306/books_tracker_s3
SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=admin
SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=your_db_password
APP_STORAGE_S3_REGION=eu-central-1
APP_STORAGE_S3_BUCKET=your-bucket-name
APP_STORAGE_S3_ACCESS_KEY=your_access_key
APP_STORAGE_S3_SECRET_KEY=your_secret_key

Spring Boot maps environment variables to properties automatically
(APP_STORAGE_S3_REGION → app.storage.s3.region). The Docker full-stack compose
files use this exact same mechanism for local development — see
Running Everything in Docker above.

repos.readme:
springboot-cicd-fabric8-jenkins-dockerhub

A small, deliberately simple Spring Boot service used as a hands-on reference for a full local CI/CD flow:
GitHub -> Jenkins -> Maven -> Flyway/MySQL -> fabric8 (Docker build) -> DockerHub -> docker-compose.

The domain (a single Product entity) is intentionally trivial. The point of this project isn't the
business logic - it's demonstrating, end to end, how the pieces of a real CI/CD pipeline fit together and
in what order.

Tech stack

Concern Tool
Language / framework Java 17, Spring Boot 3.3
Persistence Spring Data JPA / Hibernate, MySQL 8.0
Schema migrations Flyway
Mapping MapStruct + Lombok
API docs springdoc-openapi (Swagger UI)
Containerization Docker, fabric8 docker-maven-plugin
CI/CD orchestration Jenkins (Pipeline as Code via Jenkinsfile)
Image registry DockerHub
Local orchestration Docker Compose
Testing JUnit 5, H2 (in-memory)

Architecture at a glance

flowchart LR
    Dev[Developer] -->|git push| GH[GitHub]
    GH -->|checkout| Jenkins
    subgraph Jenkins Pipeline
        B1[mvn clean package] --> B2[unit tests - H2]
        B2 --> B3[fabric8 docker:build]
        B3 --> B4[fabric8 docker:push]
    end
    Jenkins -->|docker.sock| Docker[Host Docker Daemon]
    B4 -->|push image| DH[DockerHub]
    DH -->|pull image| Compose[docker compose up]
    Compose --> App[fabric8app container]
    App -->|Flyway migrate + validate| MySQL[(MySQL 8.0)]
Loading

Jenkins itself runs as a container, alongside mysql and fabric8app, all defined in the same
compose.yml. It reaches the host's Docker daemon through a mounted /var/run/docker.sock
(Docker-outside-of-Docker), so it can build and push images without needing Docker installed inside its
own container, and without needing the docker CLI at all - the fabric8 plugin talks to the daemon
directly over that socket.

The full flow, in order

A. Local build loop (no Jenkins involved)

  1. Write code.
  2. mvn clean test - compiles, runs unit tests against H2 (fast, zero external dependencies).
  3. mvn clean package - produces the runnable jar.
  4. mvn clean package docker:build - fabric8 plugin reads src/main/docker/Dockerfile, builds the image,
    tags it vladbogdadocker/fabric8app:<tag> and :latest.
  5. docker compose up mysql fabric8app - brings up MySQL (waits for its healthcheck), then the app.
    On boot, Flyway runs first (applies V1__init_product_table.sql if not already applied), then
    Hibernate validates the Product entity matches that schema (ddl-auto=validate - fails fast on
    drift instead of silently altering the table).

B. CI loop (Jenkins)

  1. Push to GitHub.
  2. Jenkins pipeline job (Pipeline script from SCM) checks out the repo, reads the Jenkinsfile.
  3. Stage 1 - inject jdk21 / maven3 tools (configured once via Jenkins UI, not baked into the image),
    print mvn --version.
  4. Stage 2 - mvn clean package: compile + unit tests (H2, same as local step 2).
  5. Stage 3 - archive the jar, publish JUnit results.
  6. Stage 4 - mvn docker:build: fabric8 builds the image over the mounted docker.sock.
  7. Stage 5 - mvn docker:push: pushes to DockerHub, authenticated via a Jenkins credential
    (dockerhub-credentials) injected as -Ddocker.username / -Ddocker.password.

C. Closing the loop

  1. docker compose pull fabric8app && docker compose up -d fabric8app - pulls the image Jenkins just
    built and pushed (not the locally-built one from step 4), proving the whole chain actually produces a
    working, deployable artifact.

Local setup

Prerequisites

  • JDK 17
  • Maven 3.9+
  • Docker Desktop running

Run tests only (no infra)

mvn clean test

Build the image and run app + MySQL

mvn clean package docker:build
docker compose up mysql fabric8app
  • App: http://localhost:8089
  • Swagger UI: http://localhost:8089/swagger-ui/index.html
  • Actuator: http://localhost:8089/actuator/info
  • MySQL is reachable on the host at localhost:3307 (mapped from container port 3306 - 3306 is often
    already taken by a local MySQL install).

Bring up Jenkins too

docker compose up -d jenkins
docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword

Open http://localhost:8080, unlock with that password, install suggested plugins.

One-time tool configuration (Manage Jenkins -> Tools):

  • JDK install named exactly jdk21 - must be a Linux build (e.g. Temurin x64_linux), not Windows,
    even though you're configuring it from a Windows browser. The auto-installer can default to the wrong
    platform (see Troubleshooting).
  • Maven install named exactly maven3 (Apache, 3.9.x) - platform-independent, no gotcha here.

One-time credential (Manage Jenkins -> Credentials -> System -> Global credentials):

  • Kind: Username with password
  • Username: your DockerHub username
  • Password: a DockerHub access token with Read & Write scope (not your account password, and not a
    read-only token - see Troubleshooting)
  • ID: exactly dockerhub-credentials

Pipeline job: New Item -> Pipeline -> Pipeline script from SCM -> Git -> this repo's URL,
branch */main, script path Jenkinsfile.

Testing strategy

Unit tests run against H2, entirely isolated from MySQL/Flyway (spring.flyway.enabled=false in
src/test/resources/application.properties). This keeps the test stage in Jenkins fast and dependency-free.

Known gap: this means Flyway's actual MySQL-flavored migration SQL is never exercised in an automated
test - only at real app startup. Closing that gap is exactly what Testcontainers is for (spin up a real,
throwaway MySQL container per test run, apply the real Flyway migration, test against it) - deliberately
left out of this round to keep the CI/CD flow itself the focus, and is the natural next iteration on this
project.

Deliberate simplifications (and why)

  • Single entity domain. The goal is demonstrating pipeline mechanics, not business complexity.
  • Jenkins on the built-in node, not a distributed agent. Jenkins itself warns about this
    ("running builds on the built-in node may be insecure") - correct advice for production, unnecessary
    complexity for a local learning setup.
  • Jenkins reaches Docker via a mounted host socket, running as root in the container. Simple and
    standard for local setups; in a real environment you'd scope this more carefully (rootless Docker,
    a dedicated docker-group GID mapping, or a remote Docker daemon over TLS).
  • No Docker-in-Docker. Not needed - the fabric8 plugin's pure-Java Docker client talks straight to the
    socket, so there's no docker CLI dependency inside the Jenkins container at all.

Troubleshooting log (real issues hit while building this)

These are kept here deliberately - they're a more honest record of a working CI/CD setup than a doc that
pretends everything worked on the first try.

Jenkins UI in Russian

Jenkins defaults to the browser's Accept-Language header. Fix: Manage Jenkins -> System -> Locale ->
set Default Language to en, check "Ignore browser preference and force this language for all users".

"Java 17 support in Jenkins has ended" + outdated core warnings

The stock jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk17 image was running a controller JVM version Jenkins itself stopped
supporting. Fixed by switching the compose image to jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21 and recreating the
container (docker compose up -d --force-recreate jenkins). The jenkins_home named volume preserves all
configuration across this change - only the container is recreated, not the data.

JDK tool auto-installer picked a Windows binary

Configuring the jdk21 tool from a Windows machine, Jenkins' installer suggested a
..._windows_hotspot...zip archive - but the controller runs inside a Linux container. Running that
build would have failed trying to execute a Windows binary on Linux. Fixed by manually pointing the
installer at the Linux x64 .tar.gz build instead (or using the dedicated Adoptium installer type, which
detects platform correctly on its own).

docker:push failing with "Error looking security dispatcher" (NoSuchElementException, SecDispatcher)

Caused by an old docker-maven-plugin version (0.39.0, from 2019) that always attempts to resolve a
Maven password-decryption component before pushing - even for plain-text passwords passed via
-Ddocker.password. That component lookup was broken for this Maven/plugin combination. Fixed by
upgrading the plugin to 0.48.1, which removed the direct dependency on that component entirely
(confirmed via the plugin's own changelog: "Move off direct SecDispatcher use").

docker:push failing with "authentication required - access token has insufficient scopes"

The DockerHub access token used for the dockerhub-credentials Jenkins credential was created with
read-only scope. Pushing requires Read & Write. Fixed by regenerating the token with the correct
scope and updating the Jenkins credential.

(Noted, not yet fixed) Groovy String interpolation warning on the push stage

Warning: A secret was passed to "sh" using Groovy String interpolation, which is insecure.

The Jenkinsfile currently embeds ${DOCKERHUB_CREDENTIALS_PSW} directly into a Groovy string passed to
sh. This doesn't block the build, but the secret can end up more exposed than necessary (e.g. in
process listings). The safer pattern is Jenkins' withCredentials block with single-quoted shell strings,
which avoids Groovy-side interpolation of the secret entirely - a good next hardening step.

Possible next steps

  • Testcontainers-backed integration tests (real MySQL + real Flyway migration, per test run)
  • withCredentials-based secret handling in the Jenkinsfile (see above)
  • Distributed Jenkins agent instead of the built-in node
  • GitHub webhook trigger instead of manual "Build Now"

repos.readme:
Token Bucket Rate Limiter

A Spring Boot + Kafka (KRaft) demo of the token bucket rate limiting
pattern - built to understand the mechanism by implementing it, not just
reading about it.

What this investigates

Rate limiting is easy to describe and easy to get subtly wrong. The
questions this project set out to answer, concretely:

  • What does "reject early, before touching the database" actually look
    like in code - not as a principle, but as the literal order of
    operations in a controller?
  • Does keying the limiter per client (not per server) actually isolate
    one bad actor from everyone else, or is that just a claim?
  • Under real concurrent load, does a rate limiter stay cheap to run, or
    does the limiting itself become the bottleneck?
  • What's the actual difference between a burst limit and a sustained
    rate limit, measured, not diagrammed?

Why

This started from an article on token bucket rate limiting and became a
test of whether the pattern holds up outside of a diagram: real Kafka
standing in for a downstream system that can only take a few hundred
requests a second, a real HTTP client (JMeter) capable of misbehaving on
purpose, and a live dashboard to watch the bucket drain and refill in
real time instead of inferring it from logs.

Architecture

Client
  |
  v
POST /api/orders  --(token bucket check, keyed by clientId)-->
  |                                                    |
  | tokens available                     no tokens available
  v                                                    v
Kafka topic "orders"                        429 + Retry-After
  |                                        (Kafka never touched)
  v
Slow consumer (simulated DB, ~500ms/msg)

Every accepted or rejected request also fires a metrics event over
Server-Sent Events, which a static dashboard renders live as a per-client
token bucket.

Stack

Concern Choice
Language / runtime Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.0
Messaging Apache Kafka, KRaft mode (no Zookeeper) - confluentinc/cp-kafka:8.0.0
Rate limiting Bucket4j 8.19.0
Live updates Server-Sent Events (no WebSocket needed for one-way data)
Dashboard Static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no build step
Load testing Apache JMeter, three test plans with different scenarios
Kafka admin/visualization Conduktor

Key decisions and why

  • In-memory bucket, one per clientId. A ConcurrentHashMap<String, Bucket>
    in a single instance. This is explicitly not distributed - a
    Redis-backed bucket is the natural extension for a multi-instance
    deployment, but was deliberately left out to keep the core mechanism
    the focus.
  • Rejection happens before any Kafka interaction. The rate limit
    check is the first line in the controller. An out-of-tokens client
    never causes a Kafka write, matching the actual point of the pattern:
    the expensive path should be the one guarded, not the one that runs
    regardless.
  • Retry-After is computed, not hardcoded. It comes directly from
    Bucket4j's ConsumptionProbe.getNanosToWaitForRefill(), so a client
    that respects the header is told exactly when to come back.
  • Kafka's consumer does a literal Thread.sleep(), standing in for
    a slow database. No real database is used - the pipeline (accept /
    reject / queue / process) is the subject of this project, not
    persistence.
  • Metrics are in-memory counters with no persistence. A dashboard
    opened mid-session gets current totals via an initial snapshot event,
    but not full historical per-client data from before it connected -
    an accepted tradeoff of keeping the metrics layer simple.

Running it

docker compose up -d        # Kafka (KRaft) + Conduktor
mvn spring-boot:run         # the app

Then open http://localhost:8080 for the dashboard, and see
additional_docs/jmeter-tests-readme.md for the three load test scenarios and
what each one is meant to prove.

Full part-by-part build notes (how each piece was put together, and the
debugging along the way) are in BUILD_GUIDE.md.

What it deliberately doesn't cover

  • Distributed rate limiting (Redis or otherwise) across multiple app
    instances
  • Persistence or durability of orders/metrics
  • Authentication or authorization on the API
  • Horizontal scaling of the app itself

These are the natural next steps if this were taken toward production,
not gaps found by accident.

Sample results

From a JMeter run at 100 req/s (50 threads) against a single client,
bucket capacity 5, refill 1 token/2s:

  • 99.38% of requests rejected (429), matching the theoretical max
    of ~20 allowed requests over 30 seconds (5 initial + 30s × 0.5/s refill)
  • Average response latency: 1ms, even at the rejection rate above -
    the limiter stayed cheap under load rather than becoming the bottleneck
    itself
  • A second client, run concurrently at its sustained rate (0.5 req/s),
    showed 0% errors in the same time window - confirming per-client
    isolation under real concurrent load, not just in isolated tests

📚 EduFlow - Education Management System





A full-featured Learning Management System (LMS) built with Spring Boot

📖 Overview

EduFlow is a comprehensive educational platform that enables seamless management of courses, students, instructors, and assignments. Built with modern Java technologies and featuring an Apple-inspired dark mode UI.

🎯 Key Functionality

  • Three User Roles: Admin, Instructor, Student with role-based access control
  • Course Management: Create, organize, and manage courses with modules and assignments
  • Assignment System: Submit work, grade submissions, provide feedback
  • Progress Tracking: Real-time progress calculation and grade analytics
  • Email Notifications: Automated emails for enrollment, grading, and reminders
  • File Upload/Download: Secure file handling for assignment submissions

👨‍🏫 For Instructors

  • Create and manage courses, modules, and assignments
  • Grade student submissions with detailed feedback
  • View student progress and course analytics
  • Post announcements to enrolled students
  • Download student submissions

👨‍🎓 For Students

  • Browse and enroll in courses
  • Submit assignments with file uploads
  • View grades and instructor feedback
  • Track course progress
  • Update profile and change password
  • View submission history

  • Course monitoring

repos.readme:
SSO with Keycloak — Spring Boot Demo

This module demonstrates Single Sign-On (SSO) using Keycloak as the Identity Provider (IdP)
and two separate Spring Boot applications as protected clients.

SCREENSHOTS











What is SSO and why does it matter?

Single Sign-On means a user logs in once and gains access to multiple independent applications — without
being asked to log in again for each one.

You experience SSO every day: logging into Google once lets you use Gmail, Drive, and YouTube without re-entering
your password. That is SSO in action.

In this demo:

  • Professor App (port 8082) — accessible only to users with the PROFESSOR role
  • Student App (port 8081) — home page accessible to both roles; Manage Students restricted to PROFESSOR
  • Keycloak (port 8080) — the central Identity Provider that holds user accounts and roles

Once a user logs in through Keycloak on one app, visiting the second app requires no second login.
Logging out from either app terminates the Keycloak session for both.

How it works — the full flow

Browser → Spring App → Keycloak → Spring App → Protected Page

Here is what happens step by step when you open /home on the Professor App for the first time:

  1. Browser hits /home — Spring Security sees the request is unauthenticated
  2. Redirect to Keycloak — Spring sends the browser to Keycloak's login page at
    http://localhost:8080/realms/university-realm/protocol/openid-connect/auth
  3. User logs in on Keycloak — Keycloak validates the credentials against its own user store
  4. Authorization code returned — Keycloak redirects the browser back to
    http://localhost:8082/login/oauth2/code/keycloak with a short-lived code
  5. Token exchange — Spring Boot (behind the scenes, server-to-server) sends that code to Keycloak
    and receives an ID Token (who you are) and an Access Token (what you can do)
  6. Roles extracted — the oidcUserService() bean reads realm_access.roles from the token
    and registers them as Spring Security GrantedAuthority objects
  7. Session established — Spring Security stores the authenticated user in the HTTP session
  8. User reaches /home — @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('PROFESSOR')") passes ✅

When the same user then opens the Student App:

  1. Browser hits /home on port 8081 — unauthenticated, redirected to Keycloak
  2. Keycloak checks its own session — the user is already logged in (SSO session cookie exists)
  3. Keycloak skips the login form and immediately issues tokens for the Student App client
  4. User lands on /home without ever seeing a login page again ✅

Why OAuth2 / OIDC and not form login?

The original codebase had UserDetailsServiceImpl, UserService, and User/Roles entities — a classic
Spring form-login setup where your app manages passwords in its own database.

That approach has problems at scale:

  • Every app needs its own user table and password logic
  • Users must maintain separate credentials per app
  • No central place to revoke access or enforce MFA

OAuth2 with OIDC (OpenID Connect) solves this by delegating authentication entirely to Keycloak:

  • Your apps store no passwords
  • Keycloak issues a signed JWT containing the user's identity and roles
  • All apps in the same realm share one login session → SSO

The UserDetailsServiceImpl, UserService, and database entities were deleted in this refactor because
they are simply not needed. Keycloak is the source of truth for identity.

Key concept: the oidcUserService() bean

@Bean
public OAuth2UserService<OidcUserRequest, OidcUser> oidcUserService() {
    OidcUserService delegate = new OidcUserService();
    return (userRequest) -> {
        OidcUser oidcUser = delegate.loadUser(userRequest);

        Map<String, Object> realmAccess = oidcUser.getClaimAsMap("realm_access");
        List<String> roles = (List<String>) realmAccess.getOrDefault("roles", List.of());

        Collection<GrantedAuthority> authorities = roles.stream()
            .map(SimpleGrantedAuthority::new)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

        return new DefaultOidcUser(authorities, oidcUser.getIdToken(), oidcUser.getUserInfo());
    };
}

Without this bean, @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('PROFESSOR')") would always fail — Spring Security
would have no knowledge of your Keycloak roles. This bean is the bridge:

  • Keycloak puts roles in the token under realm_access.roles
  • This bean reads them and wraps each one as a SimpleGrantedAuthority
  • Spring Security can then evaluate hasAuthority(...) checks normally

Keycloak setup checklist

Before running the apps, verify the following in your Keycloak admin (http://localhost:8080):

Realm

  • university-realm exists

Clients

  • professor-app client created
    • Valid redirect URI: http://localhost:8082/login/oauth2/code/keycloak

  • STUDENT role created at realm level

  • Student user → Role mappings → Realm roles → STUDENT assigned

Token mapper (critical)

  • For each client: Client scopes → <client>-dedicated → Add mapper → Realm Roles
    • Token Claim Name: realm_access.roles
    • Add to ID token: ON
    • Add to access token: ON
    • Add to userinfo: ON

Without the Realm Roles mapper, realm_access will be null in the token and the app will throw
a NullPointerException during login.

How to run

# Terminal 1 — Keycloak (already running)
# http://localhost:8080

# Terminal 2 — Professor App
cd professor-app
./mvnw spring-boot:run

# Terminal 3 — Student App
cd student-app
./mvnw spring-boot:run

# Terminal 4 — Auth Service (registration)
cd auth-service
./mvnw spring-boot:run

Registration UI: http://localhost:8083/register

Testing SSO — step by step

Test 1 — Basic login and role enforcement (Professor App)

  1. Open http://localhost:8082/home in a browser
  2. Expect: Redirect to Keycloak login page
  3. Log in as your professor user
  4. Expect: Redirected to http://localhost:8082/home — welcome page with username visible
  5. Click Manage Students
  6. Expect: Page loads — professor role is present ✅

Test 2 — Role enforcement (Student App)

  1. Open http://localhost:8081/home (in the same browser — SSO will kick in)
  2. Expect: No login prompt — you land directly on the home page (SSO) ✅
  3. Click Manage Students (PROFESSOR only)
  4. Expect: Access Denied page — or if you are logged in as a student user, try that user here ✅

Test 3 — SSO proof

This is the key test that proves SSO is working.

  1. Clear all browser cookies / use a fresh browser
  2. Open http://localhost:8082/home — log in as professor user
  3. Without logging out, open a new tab: http://localhost:8081/home
  4. Expect: You arrive at the Student App home page with no login prompt ✅
    — one Keycloak session, two apps, zero extra logins

Test 4 — SSO logout propagation

  1. While logged into both apps, click Logout on either one
  2. In the other tab, navigate to /home
  3. Expect: Redirected to Keycloak login page — the session is gone for both apps ✅

Test 5 — Cross-role access (bonus)

  1. Log in to Student App as the professor user
  2. Navigate to /manage-students
  3. Expect: Page loads — the PROFESSOR role from Keycloak works in both apps ✅

Auth Service — custom registration

The auth-service (port 8083) is a dedicated Spring Boot application that handles user registration
without using the Keycloak UI. Student and Professor App users are created here and immediately appear
in Keycloak's university-realm — ready to log in via SSO.

Why a separate service?

Separating registration from the protected apps keeps each app focused on one responsibility. The
student-app and professor-app know nothing about how users are created — they only care about validating
the JWT they receive from Keycloak. This is the standard microservice pattern for identity management.

How registration works

Browser → POST /api/auth/register → AuthServiceImpl → Keycloak Admin REST API
                                                            ↓
                                                    1. Create user
                                                    2. Set password
                                                    3. Assign realm role

The service uses the Keycloak Admin Client — a Java library that wraps Keycloak's Admin REST API.
It authenticates with Keycloak using admin-cli credentials from the master realm (the admin realm),
then performs all operations against university-realm.

Role-based registration rules

Role Email requirement Invite code required
STUDENT Any valid email No
PROFESSOR Must end with @university.com Yes (PROF2026)

These rules are enforced in AuthServiceImpl.validateRoleRules() before any call is made to Keycloak.
If a user tries to claim PROFESSOR without a university email or the correct invite code, they get a
400 Bad Request — Keycloak is never contacted. This prevents privilege escalation.

The three-step Keycloak Admin flow

Every registration goes through exactly three Admin API calls:

// Step 1 — Create the user, get back a 201 with Location header
Response response = usersResource.create(user);
String userId = extractUserIdFromLocation(response);   // parse UUID from Location URL

// Step 2 — Set the password (separate call — Keycloak separates identity from credentials)
usersResource.get(userId).resetPassword(credential);

// Step 3 — Assign the realm role by name
RoleRepresentation role = realmResource.roles().get(roleName).toRepresentation();
realmResource.users().get(userId).roles().realmLevel().add(List.of(role));

The reason password is a separate call is intentional in Keycloak's design — it lets admins create
users first and set credentials later (e.g. send a "set your password" email). In this service we do
both immediately.

Configuration

All registration rules are config-driven in application.yml — no hard-coded strings in Java:

app:
  keycloak:
    server-url: http://localhost:8080
    realm: university-realm
    admin:
      client-id: admin-cli
      username: your-credentials
      password: your-credentials

registration:
  professor-email-domain: "@university.com"
  professor-invite-code: PROF2026

To change the invite code or allowed email domain, edit application.yml and restart. No code changes needed.

Custom login theme

When users are redirected to Keycloak for authentication, they see the university-theme — a fully
custom login UI that matches the Bootstrap 4 style used across the student-app, professor-app, and
auth-service pages.

Why NOT to host your own login form in Spring Boot

A common mistake is to build a Spring Boot login form that collects credentials and sends them directly
to Keycloak using the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant. Do not do this.

  • ROPC is deprecated in OAuth 2.1 and disabled by default in newer Keycloak versions
  • It bypasses all of Keycloak's security features: MFA, brute-force lockout, suspicious login detection
  • It breaks SSO — each app would have its own login form with no shared session
  • The user's password travels through your app server instead of going directly to Keycloak

The correct approach is a Keycloak login theme — FreeMarker templates that Keycloak renders
instead of its default pages. The OAuth2 redirect flow stays 100% identical, only the visual changes.

Theme folder structure

keycloak-26.x/themes/university-theme/
├── theme.properties
└── login/
    ├── login.ftl                  # Custom login form — standalone HTML
    ├── template.ftl               # Base layout macro used by other pages
    ├── logout-confirm.ftl         # Auto-submits logout confirmation
    ├── info.ftl                   # Post-logout redirect page
    ├── error.ftl                  # Error page
    ├── login-update-profile.ftl   # Profile completion on first login
    └── resources/
        └── css/
            └── login.css          # Custom styles matching Bootstrap 4

Important for Keycloak 26: The ThemeTemplateLoader does not inherit .ftl files from the
parent theme. Every template that can be rendered during the login/logout flow must be physically
present in your theme folder. Only messages and static resources (CSS, images) are inherited from
parent=keycloak.

What each file does

login.ftl is written as a complete standalone HTML file (no #import of template.ftl) because
Keycloak 26's FreeMarker loader resolves #import statements only within your own theme folder.
All other pages use <#import "template.ftl" as layout> normally since template.ftl is present.

logout-confirm.ftl auto-submits the Keycloak logout confirmation form via JavaScript — no "Are you
sure?" click required. A <noscript> fallback button is included for JS-disabled browsers.

login-update-profile.ftl is shown on first login when a user's profile is incomplete (no
firstName/lastName set at registration time). Keycloak's built-in Verify Profile required
action triggers this page automatically. Users fill in their name once and are never asked again.

Portal context on the login page

The login page uses client.clientId from the FreeMarker model to detect which portal triggered
the login redirect and shows a colour-coded badge:

🎓 Student Portal          👨‍🏫 Professor Portal
[ Signing in to: 🎓 Student Portal ]   (blue badge)
[ Signing in to: 👨‍🏫 Professor Portal ] (green badge)

After a failed login attempt, a hint appears suggesting the other portal in case the user has the
right credentials but hit the wrong app:

💡 Have a professor account? Try the 👨‍🏫 Professor Portal instead.

Register link on the login page

When User Registration is enabled in the realm (Realm Settings → Login → User registration: ON),
a "Don't have an account? Register here" link appears at the bottom of the login form. This link
points directly to http://localhost:8083/register (the auth-service), not to Keycloak's built-in
registration UI.

Deploy steps

  1. Copy the university-theme folder into keycloak-26.x/themes/
  2. Keycloak Admin → university-realm → Realm Settings → Themes → Login Theme → university-theme
  3. Save and restart Keycloak

OIDC RP-Initiated Logout

Both Spring Boot apps use OIDC RP-Initiated Logout via Spring Security's
OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler. This is the correct approach for Keycloak 18 and later.

How it works

User clicks Logout
  → Spring invalidates the local HTTP session
  → OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler reads end_session_endpoint
    from Keycloak's OpenID discovery document automatically
  → Sends id_token_hint + post_logout_redirect_uri to Keycloak
  → Keycloak validates the token and ends the SSO session for ALL apps
  → Browser redirects to post_logout_redirect_uri (http://localhost:808X)
  → Spring sees unauthenticated request → redirects to /home → login page ✅

Why not the legacy logout URL

The old pattern used a hardcoded logout URL with a redirect_uri query parameter:

http://localhost:8080/realms/university-realm/protocol/openid-connect/logout
    ?redirect_uri=http://localhost:8082

Keycloak 18+ requires an id_token_hint parameter for automatic redirect on this endpoint.
Without it, Keycloak shows an intermediate confirmation page and then lands on the Keycloak
account console instead of your app.

Implementation in SecurityConfig

private final ClientRegistrationRepository clientRegistrationRepository;

public SecurityConfig(ClientRegistrationRepository clientRegistrationRepository) {
    this.clientRegistrationRepository = clientRegistrationRepository;
}

@Bean
public OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler oidcLogoutSuccessHandler() {
    OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler handler =
        new OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler(clientRegistrationRepository);
    handler.setPostLogoutRedirectUri("http://localhost:8082"); // or 8081 for student-app
    return handler;
}

ClientRegistrationRepository is auto-created by Spring Boot from application.yml. Injecting it
into SecurityConfig via constructor gives the logout handler everything it needs to build the
correct end-session URL at runtime — including the id_token_hint from the current user's session.

Required Keycloak Admin configuration

Each client must whitelist the post_logout_redirect_uri:

Keycloak Admin → university-realm → Clients

Athlete Monitor — Real-Time Player Tracking System

Athlete Monitor is a real-time, production-grade athlete tracking system that simulates and visualizes physiological data from up to 11 football players simultaneously. It provides sports scientists, coaches, and medical staff with instant visibility into player fatigue, injury risk, and performance metrics during training sessions or live matches.
Built with Java 17, Spring Boot 3.2, Apache Kafka, and WebSocket.

What it is and how does it work entirely

A real-time web application that simulates GPS + heart rate sensors from 11 football players, streams that data through Apache Kafka, processes it in Spring Boot, and pushes live updates to a dashboard over WebSocket. Coaches see every player on a pitch-formation view with colour-coded risk levels. Clicking a player opens a live chart showing speed and heart rate over the last 30 seconds.

Fewster — URL Shortener

A production-grade URL shortening web application built with Spring Boot, Spring Security, Thymeleaf, MySQL, and Flyway. Designed as a portfolio project demonstrating clean architecture, layered exception handling, Docker containerisation, and a professional dark-theme UI.

Overview

Fewster lets users shorten long URLs into compact short links, track how many times each link has been clicked, and manage their links from a personal dashboard. Unauthenticated visitors can try the shortener on the home page without registering.

The project is built to portfolio-grade standards: typed exception hierarchy, @Transactional service layer, Flyway-managed schema versioning, BCrypt password hashing, Spring Security with per-user resource ownership, and a fully custom dark-navy CSS design system.

  • URL shortening — MD5-based hash algorithm with collision detection and configurable retry budget
  • Click tracking — every redirect increments a persistent click counter

  • Per-user CRUD — create, view, inline-edit, and delete your own short links
  • Account settings — change username (re-authenticates in-place) or change password (forces re-login)
  • Typed exception layer — FewsterException base class with seven typed subclasses, each carrying its own HttpStatus
  • Flyway migrations — full schema version history from V1 through V8

DB_PASSWORD=your_secure_password

3. Start the application

docker compose up -d

Docker will pull the image from Docker Hub, start MySQL, wait for it to be healthy, then start the app.

4. Open in browser

http://localhost:8081

5. Stop the application

docker compose down          # stops containers, data is preserved
docker compose down -v       # stops containers AND deletes all data

Run locally (dev profile)

Prerequisites: Java 17, Maven, MySQL 8.0 running locally.

1. Create the database

CREATE DATABASE fewsterdb;

2. Configure datasource

In application-dev.yml, uncomment the local datasource block and set your credentials:

url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/fewsterdb?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true&useSSL=false&allowPublicKeyRetrieval=true
username: root
password: your_password

3. Run

Database Migrations

Schema is managed exclusively by Flyway. Hibernate is set to validate in all profiles — it never modifies the schema.

Version Description
V1 Create url table
V2 Create users table
V3 Widen column types in users
V4 Add user_id FK to url, indexes
V5 Make user_id NOT NULL, remove orphaned rows
V6 Insert demouser account
V7 Fix demo user password (BCrypt hash)
V8 Add index on users.username

Security

  • Passwords are hashed with BCryptPasswordEncoder (strength 10)
  • Each user can only access and modify their own URLs — ownership is checked on every read, update, and delete operation
  • The demouser account is used for unauthenticated demo shortenings on the home page — it cannot log in interactively
  • Session is invalidated on logout (JSESSIONID cookie deleted)
  • Password change forces an immediate logout and re-authentication
  • Username change re-authenticates the Spring Security context in-place (no logout required)
  • CSRF is disabled (stateful session app without CSRF tokens in forms — re-enable for production hardening)

/dashboard/** Authenticated + ROLE_USER
/settings/** Authenticated + ROLE_USER
/api/v1/url/** Authenticated + ROLE_USER
/r/** Public

GET /r/{shortCode} Public Redirect to original URL

Docker

Image: vladbogdadocker/fewster

The Dockerfile uses a two-stage build:

  • Stage 1 (maven:3.9.6-eclipse-temurin-17) — compiles the project with mvn clean package -DskipTests
  • Stage 2 (eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine) — copies only the final JAR into a minimal Alpine JRE image

MySQL data is stored in a Docker named volume (mysql_data). The volume survives docker compose down and is only removed with docker compose down -v.

A full-stack Spring Boot web application for tracking football league statistics — players, clubs, match days, seasons, standings, and more.
